paragraphs.heading: Laws carved in stone
paragraphs.text: The Code of Hammurabi is a Babylonian legal text written around 1753 BC. It is one of the best-known law texts of the ancient Near East. It is in the Old Babylonian dialect of Akkadian, and it is said to be the work of Hammurabi, sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon. Its main copy is carved into a basalt stone, called a stele, which stands 2.25 m tall and is now kept in the Louvre Museum.

paragraphs.heading: Who Hammurabi was
paragraphs.text: Hammurabi ruled Babylon from about 1792 to about 1750 BC. When he took the throne from his father Sin-Muballit, Babylon had little local power, and the leading ruler nearby was Rim-Sin of Larsa. Hammurabi waited until Rim-Sin was old, then seized his land in one quick campaign while keeping its organisation in place. He later betrayed allies in Eshnunna, Elam and Mari to take their lands as well. Through war, diplomacy and treachery he made Babylon the dominant power on the Mesopotamian plain.

paragraphs.heading: A king who talked of justice
paragraphs.text: Despite his aggressive dealings with other states, his letters suggest he cared about the welfare of his many subjects and took an interest in law and justice. He paid for large building works, and in his letters he often calls himself the shepherd of his people. In the Code's prologue he claims the gods gave him his rule so that the strong could not oppress the weak. Justice is a theme that runs through both the prologue and the epilogue.

paragraphs.heading: What the stele shows
paragraphs.text: The top of the stele shows Hammurabi in carved relief beside Shamash, who was the Babylonian god of the sun and of justice. Beneath it run about 4,130 lines of cuneiform text. A fifth of that text is a prologue and epilogue in poetic style, and the other four fifths are what are usually called the laws. Near the bottom, seven columns of laws were polished away in ancient times. The stele was found in three large pieces and put back together.

paragraphs.heading: If this, then that
paragraphs.text: The laws are casuistic, which here means each is set out as a conditional sentence of the form “if ... then”. They cover a wide range of life, including criminal law, family law, property law and commercial law.

paragraphs.heading: Taken as plunder
paragraphs.text: The stele was rediscovered in 1901 at Susa, an ancient Elamite city in what is now Khuzestan Province, Iran. It had been carried there as plunder 600 years after it was made. Mesopotamian scribes copied and studied the text for more than a thousand years. Copies of the stele now stand in many places, including the United Nations headquarters in New York, Berlin's Pergamon Museum and an institute for ancient cultures at the University of Chicago.

paragraphs.heading: How scholars have read it
paragraphs.text: Modern scholars responded to the Code with admiration for its apparent fairness, its respect for the rule of law, and the complex society it revealed. Many debated how it influenced the Mosaic Law, and they soon saw the principle of lex talionis, “an eye for an eye”, behind both collections. Among Assyriologists, argument has since focused on its purpose, its principles, its language, and how it relates to older and later law collections. Outside that field, Hammurabi counts as a major figure in legal history, and the text is treated as a true legal code.

paragraphs.heading: Part of a larger legal world
paragraphs.text: Thousands of documents from the practice of law survive from before and during the Old Babylonian period. They include contracts, court rulings, letters about cases, and reform texts such as that of Urukagina, a king of Lagash whose reforms fought corruption. Mesopotamia has left the fullest body of law from any time before the Digest of Justinian, richer even than what survives from ancient Greece and Rome.
